resenas-google-clinica.title: How to get more Google reviews for your clinic without breaking the rules
resenas-google-clinica.subtitle: Reviews are the most valuable asset a clinic has on Google. What practices Google prohibits, how to ask correctly and 5 legal techniques you can implement this week.
resenas-google-clinica.imageAlt: Mobile screen showing five-star ratings on Google Maps for a clinic
resenas-google-clinica.quickAnswer: To get more Google reviews legally: ask at the end of treatment, send a post-visit reminder with a direct link, place a QR code in the waiting room and actively respond to existing reviews. Google prohibits incentivising reviews with discounts, buying them or selectively asking only satisfied patients.
resenas-google-clinica.excerpt: Legal techniques to get more Google reviews for your clinic, what practices Google prohibits and how to respond to negative reviews without making things worse.
resenas-google-clinica.content:
Google reviews are the most valuable asset a clinic can have online. More than a beautiful website, more than an updated Instagram. A new patient who does not know you at all makes the decision to call or not in seconds, and the first thing they look at is the reviews and the average rating. The problem is that many clinics try to get them in ways that Google penalises or that violate regulations.

In this article I explain how Google's review system works, what is prohibited and which legal, effective techniques you can implement this week.

Why Google reviews are critical for a clinic

77% of patients read online reviews before choosing a healthcare professional, according to Software Advice data. And they do not just read: the number of reviews matters as much as the average rating. A clinic with 4.8 stars and 12 reviews generates less trust than one with 4.6 stars and 94 reviews. Volume signals that you are an active business with real patients.

Reviews also affect local ranking on Google Maps: Google's local algorithm considers quantity, recency and the business's response to reviews when determining which clinic appears first when someone searches for «physiotherapist Granada» or «dentist north zone».

The real impact of going from 15 to 50 reviews

In tests carried out with clinics in medium-sized Spanish cities, going from 15 to 50 reviews with an average rating above 4.5 increased incoming calls from Google Maps by 30 to 60% in the following 3 months. Without changing anything else on the listing or the website.

What Google prohibits (and many clinics do without knowing)

Google has clear policies on reviews and enforces them with automatic removals and listing penalties. These are the most common prohibited practices:

  • Incentivising reviews with discounts or gifts: offering a discount on the next visit in exchange for a review is a direct violation of Google's policies and can result in all your listing reviews being removed.
  • Only asking satisfied patients for reviews: selecting who you ask based on whether you think the experience was good is a practice Google considers manipulation.
  • Buying reviews: there are services that sell fake reviews. Google detects them with high accuracy, removes them and penalises the listing.
  • Reviews from employees or family: Google can identify them by behavioural patterns and IP address.

5 legal and effective ways to get more reviews

1. The end of treatment or discharge moment

The best time to ask for a review is right when a patient finishes a treatment and is satisfied with the result. In person, the professional can say: «If you are happy with the result, it would really help us if you left your opinion on Google. I'll send you the link now via WhatsApp.» Immediate, natural, no pressure.

2. The post-visit reminder via WhatsApp or email

An automatic message 2-3 hours after the appointment: «Hi [name], we hope you felt comfortable during your visit. If you would like to share your experience, here is the link to our Google listing: [direct link].» High conversion rate because it arrives while the experience is still fresh.

3. The QR code in the waiting room

A poster with a QR code in reception or the waiting room that links directly to your Google listing review section. No friction: the patient scans, writes and submits. Posters with simple text («Happy with your visit? Tell us on Google») work better than elaborate designs.

4. Actively responding to existing reviews

Responding to all reviews — positive and negative — encourages other patients to leave theirs because they see the professional is active and listens. Responses to positive reviews should be personalised and brief; negative ones require professionalism and must never include clinical data for confidentiality reasons.

5. Follow-up with recurring patients

Patients who have been coming for months or years are the most loyal but the least likely to leave reviews because they already know you. A direct, personalised message has a very high conversion rate with these profiles.

How to generate a direct link to your Google reviews

In Google Business Profile, go to your listing → «Get more reviews» → copy the short link. That link takes the patient directly to the review box without having to search for your clinic. The conversion difference compared to saying «search for us on Google» is substantial.

How to respond to negative reviews without making things worse

A negative review well responded to can generate more trust than ten positive ones with no response. A potential patient who reads a complaint and sees a professional, empathetic response that reveals no patient data knows that the professional handles problems with maturity. Never include clinical information in your response, even if the patient mentioned health details in their review: that would be a confidentiality breach.

Frequently asked questions about Google reviews for clinics

Can I remove a false negative review?

You can ask Google to remove it if it violates their policies (fake review, spam, inappropriate content). Go to the review, click the three dots and select «Report a review». Google will review it but does not guarantee removal. Documenting evidence that the review is fake — the patient does not exist in your database on that date — improves the chances.

How often should I ask for reviews?

There is no fixed rule, but consistency matters more than intensity. One new review per week, regularly over months, is more effective for Google's algorithm than 20 reviews in one month followed by nothing for half a year. Recency is a relevant ranking factor.

Should I also respond to 5-star reviews?

Yes. Responding to all reviews, even positive ones, shows the business is active and that you value the time of the person who left the opinion. Avoid generic copied responses: personalise even if just with the patient's name or a reference to the service mentioned.

Do Google Maps reviews affect website ranking?

They affect ranking on Google Maps and in the local pack (the 3-listing block that appears for some searches), not directly organic website ranking. But indirectly yes: more Maps visibility → more clicks → more traffic → positive signal for the general algorithm.

How many reviews do I need to rank well on Google Maps?

It depends on local competition. In Granada, for specialities with little competition (podiatrists, speech therapists) 20-30 reviews with a good rating may be enough to appear at the top. For dentists or physiotherapists in competitive areas, you need 60-100+ reviews to compete with well-established clinics.

pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.title: Why patients don't come back to your clinic (and what you can change)
pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.subtitle: Most patients who do not return were not dissatisfied: nobody gave them a reason to come back. The 5 real reasons for drop-out and what you can change starting this week.
pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.imageAlt: Empty chair in clinic waiting room with natural light coming through the window
pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.quickAnswer: Patients do not return mainly for five reasons: no post-visit follow-up, booking the next appointment was difficult, they did not perceive enough improvement, the price surprised them, or they simply forgot and nobody reminded them. Retaining a patient costs 5 to 25 times less than acquiring a new one, making retention the most profitable investment any clinic can make.
pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.excerpt: The 5 real reasons why patients do not return to your clinic and what you can change without major investment: post-visit follow-up, booking process, price transparency and automatic reminders.
pacientes-no-vuelven-clinica.content:
There is a problem affecting almost every clinic that very few talk about openly: patients who came once, had a reasonable experience and never came back. Not because they were dissatisfied. They simply did not return. And each one represents lost revenue you will never recover.

In this article I analyse the real reasons why patients do not repeat visits, what you can do to change that dynamic without major investment, and when technology can give you a real advantage over other clinics that have not yet solved this.

The silent cost of patients who do not return

Harvard Business Review quantified it years ago and it remains true: retaining a customer costs 5 to 25 times less than acquiring a new one. In the clinical sector this translates very concretely: every new patient who walks in requires advertising, SEO or referrals. Every patient who already visited and returns costs nothing in acquisition.

A physiotherapy clinic with 100 active patients and a 50% retention rate needs to acquire 50 new patients a year just to maintain volume. With 70% retention, it only needs 30 new ones. The difference in marketing effort and cost is enormous.

What is a loyal patient actually worth?

A physiotherapy patient who comes an average of 8 sessions a year at 50 € per session generates 400 € annually. If they remain loyal for 3 years, that is 1,200 € in total. Losing them after the first visit carries an opportunity cost of 1,150 €, plus the cost of acquiring the next new patient to replace them.

The 5 real reasons why patients do not come back

1. They received no follow-up after the first visit

The most frequent reason and the most solvable. The patient came, the consultation went well, they left with the feeling they should «see how it goes» and were never heard from again. Nobody wrote to ask how they were. Nobody reminded them it made sense to return. The patient does not not want to come back: they just have no concrete reason to do so and inertia does the rest.

2. Booking the next appointment was too difficult

If coming back to your clinic requires calling during office hours, waiting to get through and coordinating a slot with the professional, many patients simply will not bother. Friction kills intention. A clinic with 24-hour online booking has a significantly higher return rate than one that only accepts phone calls during opening hours.

3. They did not perceive enough improvement in the first or second session

In specialities like physiotherapy, osteopathy or psychology, results are not immediate. If the patient does not understand why they need more sessions — and nobody explained it clearly — they drop out. Communicating the treatment plan and realistic expectations is both a clinical skill and a business one.

4. The financial proposal was unexpected

The price surprised them: either because it was not clear upfront or because the treatment plan involved a total spend they had not calculated. Price transparency — on the website, at the first consultation, in the quote — significantly reduces drop-out due to financial surprise.

5. They simply forgot and nobody reminded them

Life gets in the way. The patient intended to return, kept putting it off, and after three months no longer felt the urgency. An automatic reminder at 30, 60 or 90 days — «Hi, it has been 6 weeks since your last visit. How are you feeling?» — recovers a significant percentage of these patients without any manual effort.

What you can implement without advanced technology

Not everything requires custom software. These actions have real impact and can be implemented this week:

  • 48-hour follow-up protocol: a WhatsApp or email two days after the first visit asking how the patient is. High response rate and generates a sense of care that differentiates you from competitors.
  • Explicit treatment plan explanation: before the patient leaves the first consultation, explain how many sessions are recommended, how often and what each phase aims to achieve.
  • Visible total price: if a complete treatment costs 300 €, say so at the start. Financial surprises at the third session generate drop-out and distrust.
  • Welcome card with online booking link: a physical or digital card with a QR to your booking system and the reminder that they can book whenever they want, from their phone, without calling.

When technology makes a real difference

Once you have the human protocol working, technology multiplies its effect. An application connected to your schedule can automatically detect when a patient has not booked in more than X weeks and send them a personalised reminder. It can analyse which patient profiles have the highest drop-out risk — first visit without a follow-up appointment booked — and flag them for priority follow-up.

It can also show you data that without technology is invisible: what percentage of this month's new patients have booked a second appointment, which treatment has the highest drop-out rate, from which acquisition channel the patients who return most frequently come. With that information, your business decisions stop being intuition and become strategy.

Frequently asked questions about patient retention in clinics

What is a good retention rate for a clinic?

It depends on the speciality. In physiotherapy or psychology, where treatments are ongoing, a healthy retention rate is between 60 and 75%. For dentists, where check-ups are annual, 70-80% of patients returning the following year is the target. Below 40% in any speciality, there is something to investigate.

Can I win back patients who stopped coming months ago?

Yes. Reactivation of inactive patients is one of the highest-return actions in clinical marketing. A personalised message — «We have not heard from you in a while, how are you?» — without commercial pressure has response rates of 15-30% among patients who had not booked in more than 3 months.

How does the waiting room experience affect retention?

More than most think. Waiting time, atmosphere, reception staff attitude and ease of leaving (fast payment, next appointment booked before they go) are factors patients weigh even without verbalising them. A clinically excellent practice with a cold and slow reception has worse retention than a clinic with similar results and a carefully managed administrative experience.

What is the difference between retention and loyalty?

Retention means the patient comes back. Loyalty means they come back and also recommend you. Retention is built with follow-up and experience; loyalty is built with accumulated trust, results and the feeling that you care about their progress beyond the appointment. Spontaneous positive reviews are the clearest indicator of real loyalty.

How long does it take to improve retention after implementing these changes?

Protocol changes (48h follow-up, treatment plan explanation) have an effect within 4-8 weeks. Technology changes (automatic reminders, analytics) require 3-6 months to generate enough data to optimise. Combining both from the start is the most effective strategy.
